old: None of this is an argument against ownership, only against buying on a quoted budget that nobody has tested. Made with the full cost in view, ownership can be one of the most rewarding purchases a person makes. Made on rule-of-thumb figures and on advice from people paid only if the sale closes, it can be one of the more expensive mistakes an ultra-high-net-worth (UHNW) buyer makes.
new: None of this argues against ownership. It argues against buying on the strength of a quoted budget that nobody has tested. Made with the full cost in view, the right ownership decision is one of the great purchases a person can make. Based on untested figures and advice from parties whose fees depend on completion, it can be an expensive mistake.
reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 22: Restores the more distinctive sentence. Confirm that the assertion about completion-based remuneration is supported in this example.

old: The sale left him with cash in the low nine figures.

reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 29: Proceeds, personal cash received and a liquidity event are not synonymous. This wording is conditional on transaction records.

old: The price reduction was EUR 2.1 m, about 25 times the EUR 85,000 the survey process cost. The reduction was not a profit: the buyer still spent EUR 2.0 to 2.4 m on remediation, which it roughly covered. Against closing at the asking price without the survey, the buyer was about EUR 2.0 m better off (EUR 2.1 m less EUR 85,000). On any acquisition above about EUR 5 m, the cost of an independent survey is small against what it can find.
new: The seller reduced the price by EUR 2.1 m following the survey, approximately 25 times the EUR 85,000 survey cost. That reduction was not a profit: the buyer still faced EUR 2.0 to 2.4 m of remedial work. Any comparison with buying at the original asking price assumes that the buyer would have completed without the survey and paid for the same repairs.
reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 248: Avoid presenting the survey as generating a realised EUR 2 m return. Price reduction and repair cost must be reconciled.

old: He would have paid about EUR 2.0 m more in total than he did, after allowing for the EUR 85,000 the survey process cost. That sum would have stayed with the seller.
new: If the buyer had paid the original asking price and incurred the same repair costs, total expenditure would have been about EUR 2.0 m higher after allowing for the EUR 85,000 survey cost. This is a hypothetical comparison, not a realised saving.
reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 249: Makes the necessary assumptions explicit; do not claim the extra EUR 2 m necessarily would have gone to the seller without evidence.

old: The risk on the yard side, less covered in the trade press, has recurred through the 2020s: a yard runs into financial difficulty mid-build, and the owner is asked to inject more capital, sometimes as equity in the restructured business, or accept that the build will stop, suppliers will stop work, and the unfinished yacht will become an asset of the insolvency.
new: When a yard gets into financial difficulty during construction, it may seek additional funding from the owner or suspend work. The owner’s ability to recover the unfinished yacht and equipment depends on the contract, when title passes, any security held and the law of the country where the yacht is being built.
reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 277: The unfinished yacht does not automatically become property of the insolvency estate.

old: The EUR 1.2 m of engineering, materials and labour would have been payable under any contract. The EUR 1.4 m margin was a different matter. A specialist shipbuilding lawyer would have negotiated pre-agreed unit rates and the right to obtain third-party quotes above a threshold at heads of terms, so that the yard’s price could be checked against the rates and against other bidders. Some margin would still have been payable, but the yard could not have set it alone. The owner had instead a general clause under which the yard would charge what it considered reasonable.
new: The EUR 1.2 m attributed to engineering, materials and labour reflected the work proposed, but the amount payable could have differed under other pricing terms. The EUR 1.4 m yard margin raised a separate contractual question. Agreed unit rates and the right to obtain third-party quotations could have allowed the owner to test the price of variations. Instead, the contract permitted the yard to charge what it regarded as reasonable.
reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 322: Do not state that the underlying cost would have been payable under every possible contract; a negotiated margin cannot be assumed wholly avoidable.

old: the owner had paid approximately EUR 5.2 m in margin on variations (40 percent of EUR 13 m). The other EUR 7.8 m, the engineering and materials, would have been paid under any contract. Some margin is payable under any terms; unit rates and quote rights would have limited how much.
new: the owner had paid approximately EUR 5.2 m in margin on EUR 13 m of variations, equivalent to 40 percent. Defined pricing rules and quotation rights might have limited that margin, but the calculation alone does not establish how much could have been avoided.
reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 324: Removes unsupported claim that EUR 7.8 m would be due under any contract.

old: Yachts are refitted in cycles. Every five years a class survey requires structural and systems work, and about every ten years the finishes and major systems need substantial overhaul. Refits account for a large share of the cost of ownership, and they are where the relationship between owner, yard and project manager is most often tested.
new: Yachts are refitted at intervals dictated by their age, condition, maintenance history and intended use. Class renewal surveys take place at prescribed intervals, commonly five years under applicable rules, but the repairs required depend on the survey findings. Major refits can account for some of the largest individual costs of ownership and test the working relationship between owner, yard and project manager.
reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 353: Survey cycles are not automatic repair or ten-year replacement mandates.

old: Once the yacht was opened up the yard found work that genuinely needed doing, and the final cost was double the original quote. The four main findings added EUR 1.37 m; the rest of the increase built up under a loosely defined scope, payments tied to calendar dates, and reporting that did not track cost against budget.
new: Once the yacht was opened up, the yard found additional work and the final cost was double the original quote. Four identified findings accounted for EUR 1.37 m of the EUR 3.2 m increase. The remaining EUR 1.83 m is not itemised in this account.
reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 394: Do not assign the unaccounted EUR 1.83 m to particular causes without project evidence.

old: An overrun of 100 percent is at the high end of practitioner experience, but not unique. Of the EUR 3.2 m increase, the four findings above account for EUR 1.37 m. The rest built up with the scope loosely specified, payments tied to the calendar rather than to completed work, and oversight provided free by a party the owner did not pay.
new: The final account was approximately 100 percent above the original quote. The four findings described above total EUR 1.37 m of the EUR 3.2 m increase. The balance is not itemised here and cannot, on these figures alone, be attributed to contract terms or project controls.
reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 404: The subtraction proves an unallocated remainder, not the cause of that remainder.

old: One useful sign in interview is whether a candidate is willing to question the owner’s plans. A captain who asks how the yacht will actually be used, about the family, about the owner’s tolerance for transit days and about the refit reserve is showing
new: One useful sign in an interview is whether a captain is prepared to question the owner’s plans. A candidate who asks how the yacht will be used, who will be aboard, how much time the owner is prepared to spend in transit and what has been allowed for refits is showing

old: Getting the agreed value and its basis wrong can leave the owner eight figures short in a total loss, as the rebuild-cost example above shows, and a specialist broker is more likely to get them right.
new: The gap between an agreed insured value and the cost of replacing a yacht can be substantial following a total loss. Owners should examine the policy’s valuation basis and terms with a broker who understands large-yacht insurance.
reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 465: Removes unsupported assurance that a specialist broker is more likely to get the figures right, and does not infer a certain eight-figure payout gap.

old: Senior crew staying 5 to 8 years is usually a sign of a well-run yacht. An average stay below 2 years usually means the crew are leaving because of the captain or the owner.
new: Long service among senior crew can be a useful sign of stability. If average tenure is short, the owner should establish why. Leadership is one possible cause, alongside pay, rotation, career progression and changes in the yacht’s programme.
reason: Editorial revision, CSV row 491: Short tenure alone does not identify the captain or owner as the cause.
